title: Dashimaki Tamago
subtitle: rolled dashi omelette
excerpt: Dashimaki tamago is the Kyoto version of the Japanese rolled omelette, made with a high ratio of dashi stock added to the egg. It is lighter, more savoury and more delicate than tamagoyaki. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Dashimaki tamago is closely associated with Kyoto cooking and kaiseki cuisine. The high dashi content makes it technically harder to roll than regular tamagoyaki: the mixture is very loose and requires a confident technique and a hot pan.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Can be wrapped in a bamboo mat and pressed up to 2 hours ahead. Slice just before serving.

glossaryTerms.definition: Japanese stock made from kombu and bonito flakes. In dashimaki tamago it is added directly into the egg in a much higher ratio than in tamagoyaki, making the omelette looser and more delicate.
A style of Japanese rolled omelette from Kyoto where dashi stock is mixed into the egg at a 1:1 ratio, producing a much lighter, silkier result than sweet tamagoyaki.

content.text: in the egg mixture, making it very loose and hard to roll. The result is almost custardy inside with a lightly set exterior. Serves 4.
The pan must be very hot before the egg goes in. A cool pan will cause the loose dashi mixture to spread too thin before it can be rolled.
Gently beat the eggs with chopsticks, trying not to add air. Add the dashi, soy sauce and mirin. Stir gently to combine. Strain through a fine sieve.
Heat a small frying pan or tamagoyaki pan over medium-high heat. Add the oil and wipe with a paper towel so only a very thin film coats the surface.

Pour in one third of the egg mixture. It will be very loose. When the bottom is just barely set and the top still looks wet, quickly fold and roll from one side using a spatula. The roll will not be perfect at this stage. Slide to one end of the pan.

Oil the exposed pan surface. Pour in another third of the egg mixture, letting it flow under the first roll. Set the bottom, then roll the first roll back over the new egg, incorporating it. Repeat with the remaining mixture.
Transfer the omelette to a bamboo mat or cling film. Roll tightly and press into shape. Leave to rest for 5 minutes. Slice into 2cm rounds and serve. The centre should look slightly soft and moist.

attrs.symptom: Mixture is so liquid it cannot be rolled
attrs.cause: Pan was not hot enough when the egg went in
attrs.fix: The pan must be very hot so the bottom sets quickly. With dashi in the mix, there is little margin for error on heat.

attrs.symptom: Omelette is rubbery not custardy inside
attrs.cause: The mixture was overcooked before rolling
attrs.fix: Roll when the top is still wet. The centre should remain soft after resting. Less cooking is always better.

attrs.cause: Not pressed firmly enough in the mat or cling film, or not rested long enough
attrs.fix: Press firmly when rolling in the mat and let it rest for 5 minutes before slicing. The shape will hold.

content.text: Dashimaki tamago is a Kyoto speciality associated with refined cooking. You find it at kaiseki restaurants and in the bento boxes sold at Kyoto station. The technique is demanding. Many Japanese home cooks consider it an advanced skill worth practising. The flavour when you get it right is quite different from sweet tamagoyaki: lighter, more savoury and deeply comforting.
